As for your question, humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years. The earliest recorded observations of the night sky date back to ancient civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece. These cultures believed that the sky was a dome above the Earth, and that the stars and planets were gods or spirits.

The ancient Greeks, in particular, were fascinated by the night sky and made detailed observations of the stars and planets. They believed that the Earth was surrounded by a crystal sphere, and that the stars and planets were attached to this sphere. This idea was later challenged by the ancient Greek philosopher Aristarchus of Samos, who proposed a heliocentric model of the universe, where the Sun was at the center and the Earth and other planets orbited around it.

The concept of a blue sky outside of Earth's atmosphere is a bit more complex. In the early days, people believed that the sky was a solid dome above the Earth, and that the stars and planets were reflected off this dome. This idea was later challenged by the ancient Greek philosopher Empedocles, who proposed that the sky was a transparent dome made of a material called "aether."

The modern understanding of outer space as a vast, dark void filled with stars and galaxies developed over the course of several centuries. The first telescope was invented by Galileo Galilei in 1608, and it allowed people to see the stars and planets in greater detail. The discovery of the Moon's phases by Galileo and the observation of the phases of Venus by Johannes Kepler helped to establish the heliocentric model of the universe.

The first spacecraft, Sputnik 1, was launched by the Soviet Union in 1957, and it marked the beginning of the space age. Since then, humans have sent numerous spacecraft to explore the solar system, and we have gained a much greater understanding of the nature of outer space.

As for the color of the sky outside of Earth's atmosphere, it is actually black, not blue. The Earth's atmosphere scatters sunlight in all directions, giving the sky its blue color. However, in the vacuum of space, there is no atmosphere to scatter the light, so the sky appears black. The stars and galaxies that we see in space are actually incredibly distant, and their light has been traveling through the vacuum of space for millions or even billions of years.
